\chapter{Vi, Di --- The Shortest Pasts}
\label{ch:vi-di}
\hlchaptermodality{255}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can use the preterite of ver and dar.}

I can use the preterite of ver and dar.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[vi · di]{vi · di — the shortest pasts in the language}

\label{lesson:ES-C65-vi-di}



\begin{quote}
The \emph{-er} past, first person: \emph{comí}, with an accent, because the stress lands at the end.

Now do the same to \emph{ver}, whose stem is a single letter.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: nothing left to accent}]
\begin{quote}
\emph{ver} $\to$ \emph{\textbf{vi}}, \emph{\textbf{viste}}, \emph{\textbf{vio}}
\end{quote}

Look at \emph{vi} and \emph{vio}: \textbf{no accent}, where \emph{comí} and \emph{comió} both had one.

And the reason is not an exception. A written accent exists to say \emph{the beat is here, not where you would expect}. A word of \textbf{one syllable} has nowhere else the beat could be, so there is nothing to correct. Spanish does not spend a mark on a choice that does not exist.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: and dar, which behaves like an -er verb}]
\emph{\textbf{Dar}} means \emph{to give}. It is an \emph{-ar} verb — and in the preterite it flatly refuses to behave like one:

\begin{quote}
\emph{dar} $\to$ \emph{\textbf{di}}, \emph{\textbf{diste}}, \emph{\textbf{dio}}, \emph{\textbf{dimos}}, \emph{\textbf{disteis}}, \emph{\textbf{dieron}}
\end{quote}

Those are the \emph{-er} endings, on an \emph{-ar} verb, with the same one-syllable forms going bare. \emph{Ver} does the same in the plural: \emph{vimos}, \emph{visteis}, \emph{vieron}.

Two verbs, one shared oddity, and now the last two named irregulars of the preterite are yours.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{vi}, \emph{viste}, \emph{vio}
  \item \emph{di}, \emph{diste}, \emph{dio}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why do \emph{vi} and \emph{di} carry no accent? (\textbf{One syllable} — the beat has nowhere else to fall.)

And which endings does \emph{dar} take in the past? (The \emph{\textbf{-er}} ones, though it is an \emph{-ar} verb.)
\end{tcolorbox}
